passage:
In the seminar room of the physics department, Pankaj, a first-year, raised a point about the experiment. "The readings drift because of the temperature, so if we..."
"Yes, and we can just repeat it," said Jahnavi, a final-year student, cutting in. Others nodded. Ten minutes later Jahnavi said, "My idea is to control the temperature," and the professor wrote it down.
Pankaj felt hot, then went quiet and looked at the notes. After the session, Pankaj walked up. "Jahnavi, I said the temperature part earlier, and I was cut off. I'd like to finish my thought next time." Jahnavi paused. "You did. I'm sorry."

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say ten minutes later that the professor wrote down?
qa.a: Jahnavi said, "My idea is to control the temperature."

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling after the idea was credited to Jahnavi?
qa.a: Pankaj felt hurt and unheard, going hot and then quiet. Looking at the notes shows a wish to disappear from the discussion.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do after the session, and how did it help?
qa.a: Pankaj walked up and said the temperature point was Pankaj's and had been cut off, and asked to finish next time. Jahnavi paused, apologised and acknowledged it.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when Pankaj spoke after the session?
qa.a: Jahnavi was probably caught off guard, but then acknowledged the mistake and apologised. The calm request made it easy to accept.

grounding: A student whose points are cut off and later credited to a senior goes quiet, then asks to finish the thought.

passage:
Subject: Finishing my point in group meetings
Dear Gurleen,
I hope you are well. In Tuesday's project meeting I began to explain the survey design, but was interrupted twice, and later the same idea was presented as Rohan's. I stayed quiet, and I think I have been quiet in the last few meetings too.
I'd like to ask a small thing: could we agree that each person finishes their point before someone else answers? I am happy to write my ideas in the shared document too, so they are on record.
Thank you for listening. I would like the group to work well.
Best,
Sarika

qa.q: On which day was the project meeting where Sarika was interrupted?
qa.a: The project meeting was on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when staying quiet in the meeting?
qa.a: Sarika was hurt and discouraged, feeling unheard after the idea was credited to someone else. The email admits going quiet in later meetings too.

qa.q: What did Sarika ask for in the email, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: Sarika asked that each person finish a point before someone else answers, and offered to put ideas in the shared document. It is polite, specific and practical.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Sarika's email?
qa.a: Gurleen may be surprised but can see a clear, calm request and a wish for the group to work well. The tone makes it easy to agree.

grounding: A student whose points are repeatedly cut off and credited to someone else goes quiet, then emails to ask to finish the thought.

passage:
Tutorial lead's note, Week 6, Economics seminar
I've noticed a pattern in Group B. Sharmila, a second-year student, begins a point and Ramesh talks over her before she finishes. Today it happened four times. Twice, Ramesh later repeated her idea about rural credit almost word for word, and the group credited him.
After the second time, Sharmila stopped speaking and looked down at her notes for the rest of the session.
I stayed back with her afterwards. She said, "Maybe my English isn't clear enough." I told her it was clear; the problem was the interruptions.
She asked whether it would be rude to say, "Can I finish my point?" I said it is completely fair.
What I'll do next: I will start using a speaking order in Group B, and when an idea is repeated, I will name who said it first. I'll check in with Sharmila after next week's session.

qa.q: How many times did Ramesh talk over Sharmila today?
qa.a: Today it happened four times.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila stop speaking?
qa.a: Sharmila felt discouraged and unheard after being cut off and seeing her idea credited to Ramesh, and began doubting her English.

qa.q: What steps could help Sharmila be heard?
qa.a: Sharmila can calmly say "Can I finish my point?", and the tutorial lead's speaking order and naming who said an idea first will help too.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see the seminar discussions?
qa.a: Ramesh may see himself as an active, confident participant, perhaps not noticing he is cutting Sharmila off and taking her ideas.

grounding: An adult's note shows a student repeatedly talked over and her idea credited to someone else, and asking to finish is legitimate.

passage:
Thursday
Study group again. Every time I started explaining the circuit problem, Rafiq cut in: "Yeah, yeah, basically it's—" and then explained MY method, badly. Twice. Then the others thanked him.
By the third time I just stopped. I sat there doodling, feeling invisible, wondering if my accent makes people stop listening. Or if it's because I'm the only girl in the group.
Walking back, I was so angry I almost cried.
But then I remembered what Ammi says: "Your voice has a right to be in the room."
So tomorrow I'm going to try it. When he cuts in, I'll say, calmly, "Rafiq, can I finish? I'm nearly there." I practised it three times in the mirror. It sounds less rude than I thought.
Zainab, you're not invisible. Just interrupted.
Friday update: I said it. He actually stopped. The others listened.

qa.q: What was Zainab explaining when Rafiq cut in?
qa.a: Zainab was explaining the circuit problem.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling after being cut off three times?
qa.a: Zainab felt invisible and angry, close to tears, and doubted whether her accent or being the only girl made people stop listening.

qa.q: What made Zainab's plan work?
qa.a: She practised a calm, short line, "Rafiq, can I finish? I'm nearly there," which claimed her turn without attacking him.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when Zainab asked to finish?
qa.a: Rafiq might have felt a little surprised and embarrassed, realising he had been cutting her off.

grounding: A student repeatedly talked over goes quiet, then asks calmly to finish her point, which is legitimate.

passage: At the agriculture college in Hassan, the soil-testing group met on the verandah after lab. Hafsa began, "If we sample before the rains, the nitrogen reading—" "Yeah, yeah, basically we test early," Eshaan cut in, and the group moved on. Twice more she started; twice more he finished for her, louder. By the end she was drawing circles in her notebook. At Friday's review, Eshaan presented "his idea" of sampling before the rains. Professor Gowda nodded approvingly. Hafsa's face burned. Walking to the bus stand afterwards, her classmate Latha said, "That was your point. I heard you say it on Monday." Hafsa stopped. "He never lets me finish." "Next time, just say you'd like to finish. I'll back you." At the next meeting, when Eshaan cut in again, Hafsa said evenly, "Let me finish, please." Latha nodded. Eshaan sat back. Hafsa finished.

qa.q: Where did the soil-testing group meet?
qa.a: On the verandah after lab.

qa.q: What does Hafsa drawing circles in her notebook suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt unheard and discouraged, and had given up trying to speak in that meeting.

qa.q: What worked at the next meeting, and why?
qa.a: Hafsa calmly asked to finish, with Latha nodding support, which claimed her turn without a fight.

qa.q: Why might Latha have spoken up on the walk to the bus stand?
qa.a: Latha had heard Hafsa's idea on Monday and felt it was unfair to see it credited to Eshaan, so she wanted to back her.

grounding: Shows a student whose points are cut off and later credited to someone else going quiet, then reclaiming her turn by asking to finish.
